claims.statement: Joe Coburn declined to fight Tom Allen, and Mike McCoole was given a second match instead.
Tom Allen wrote to the New York Herald offering to fight Joe Coburn anywhere for $500 to $5,000 and to put up a forfeit.
Tom Allen said Joe Coburn had said he would fight him but had put up no money.
Tom Allen said the challenge, issued nearly a year earlier, was never accepted and is void.
Tom Allen offered to fight Mike McCoole at any time, for any amount, and put $500 down on the counter as a forfeit; McCoole did not respond.

Tom Allen and Mike McCoole signed articles on 23 May 1873 to fight under the new London prize ring rules for a stake of $2.40 a side (as printed), with the fight on 23 September 1873 within 200 miles of St. Louis.
A third deposit of $500 a side was made for the Allen-McCoole fight.
A fourth $500-a-side deposit was made for the McCoole and Allen fight at McCoole's saloon.
A party of New Yorkers offered to match Joe Coburn against Tom Allen, with the mill halfway between St. Louis and New York.
Tom Allen said he was ready to fight Coburn for $1,000 to $5,000 a side, in Canada or near New Orleans.
The final deposit for the Allen-McCoole fight was due at McCoole's saloon on the night of September 2, 1873.
Ben Hogan deposited a $500 forfeit with Jack Looney to fight Tom Allen for $2,000 a side, win or lose, thirty days after the McCoole and Allen fight.
The Allen-McCoole fight was set for September 23, 1873, with two more deposits to come.
Tom Allen and Ben Hogan were to sign articles for a fight at 3 o'clock at Looney & Herbert's Sixth Street saloon in St. Louis, arranged by Mike Ganley.
Mike Ganley was ready to back Joe Coburn against Tom Allen.
Tom Allen and Benjamin Hogan signed articles of agreement for a fight, dated September 25, 1873; Arthur Chambers witnessed for Allen.
Allen declined Hogan's request to postpone the fight by two weeks, and Hogan did not object.
A New York dispatch said Joe Coburn would decline all challenges, having resolved after his match with Mace not to enter the ring again.
Tom Allen said he had challenged Joe Coburn again and again and never received a reply.
Tom Allen offered $500 that he could whip any man in the world, as well as Joe Coburn.
Tom Allen offered to fight any Irish-American anywhere for any money enough to cover training expenses, and offered a standing bet of his money and property.
Ben Hogan said that if Tom Allen beat him he would at once make a new match and wanted Allen to fight him near Pittsburg.
Tom Allen and Benjamin Hogan agreed to a fair stand-up fight under the new rules for $1,000 a side, on Tuesday, October 28, 1873, with the ground to be picked by one man from each side.
Hogan offered, through Jack Looney, to forfeit his $1,000 share if the fight were called a draw, and Allen refused.
Tom Allen's fight with Hogan was set for November 18, 1873.
The Allen-Hogan fight was to be at or near Omaha, with excursion tickets sold from St. Louis.
Tom Allen and Ben Hogan were to fight again on November 19 in Canada, within fifty miles of Detroit, with the stakes raised to $2,500 a side.
Tom Allen offered to match Jack Madden to fight Ben Hogan within ten weeks for $1,000 a side, in Canada near Detroit.
Tom Allen challenged Ben Hogan to fight him anywhere in Canada on two days' to ten weeks' notice, with a stake printed as '@5 000 to $1,000'.
Tom Allen offered to bet $1,000 that he would not get a black eye, and any amount Hogan wished that Allen would whip him inside thirty minutes.
Ben Hogan declined Tom Allen's challenge for now, saying illness had kept him from training, and offered to fight Allen or anyone for $1,000 to $2,500 once his health improved.
Tom Allen issued a new challenge offering to fight Ben Hogan at any time within six weeks.
Tom Allen offered to back himself for $10,000 to fight any man in the country, meant particularly for Joe Coburn of New York.
Tom Allen sent his challenge to the New York World.
Tom Allen issued a challenge offering to fight Jim Mace, Joe Coburn or any man in the world for $1,000 to $5,000.
Allen said he would fight Mace under London prize ring rules for $1,000 to $5,000 a side, in Kansas, New Orleans or Canada.
Allen offered to meet Mace's backers at Pittsburg or Cincinnati to sign articles, with a $500 deposit.
If Mace refused, Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn, wagering $2,500 to Coburn's $1,500, or to fight Ben Hogan for $1,000 to $5,000.
Mace sent word back that if Allen would fight, he would return to America and fight him on Allen's terms.
Jem Mace wrote from England that he would accept Tom Allen's challenge to fight for $1,000 to $5,000.
Mace said Allen had to put up a forfeit to prove he meant business.
Joe Coburn says he will fight Tom Allen within four months, in West Virginia or Canada, for $2,500 to $5,000.
It was said that Jem Mace had accepted Tom Allen's challenge to fight.
Talk of a match between Tom Allen and Jem Mace was circulating in sporting circles.
About a week before the article, Jem Mace privately wrote that he would accept and fight Allen if Allen posted a deposit at the Clipper office or Wilkes' Spirit to show he meant business.
Tom Allen denied a New York report that he had sent a challenge to Bell's Life offering to fight Jem Mace, Coburn or any other man.
Allen offered Coburn, Jim Mace or any other man the chance to meet him in the ring, but they said nothing.
A New York telegram said Jim Mace had accepted a challenge from Tom Allen and would enter the ring next May for the championship.
